**Short answer:** *No—unless the contract is re‑structured to shift a meaningful portion of the financial risk back to the payer (or to the group through shared‑savings/stop‑loss mechanisms) and the group can build the clinical, legal, and operational infrastructure needed to manage that risk.* Below is a pragmatic “what‑if” analysis that shows why the raw numbers are not enough, what the deal should look like to be defensible, and how you can structure it so the practice remains financially viable while protecting patients and staff. --- ## 1. Quick math: Is $1,180 PMPM realistic? | Item | Calculation | Result | |------|-------------|--------| | **Monthly revenue** | 25 000 members × $1,180 /PMPM | **$29.5 M** | | **Annual revenue** | $29.5 M × 12 | **$354 M** | | **Average Medicare Advantage cost (2023)** | ~$1,200 /PMPM (national) | ~**$30 M/month** | | **Estimated cost for a primary‑care‑only group** | ~$800–$900 /PMPM (if only office visits & basic services) | $20–22 M/month | *Bottom line:* If the group is responsible for *all* Medicare services, it will need to keep total costs below $1,180 PMPM. That’s a 4‑5% margin on top of the national average cost—tight but not impossible if you can: 1. **Reduce high‑cost episodes** (hospitalizations, ED visits, specialty care). 2. **Leverage risk‑adjusted payment** so that sicker patients are compensated more. 3. **Earn quality bonuses** to offset some costs. If the group is only responsible for primary‑care services and the payer pays separately for hospital/ specialist care, then $1,180 PMPM is *excessive*—you would be overpaying by roughly 30–40%. --- ## 2. Why the raw number alone isn’t enough | Domain | Risk / Challenge | |--------|------------------| | **Clinical** | • Managing a 25k‑member panel with diverse comorbidities.
• Need for care coordination, chronic disease management, and social determinants of health (SDOH) interventions.
• Potential for higher-than-expected utilization if the payer’s network is limited. | | **Legal / Compliance** | • Medicare Conditions of Participation (CoP) & Anti‑Fraud/Abuse laws.
• Data privacy (HIPAA, HITECH).
• Liability for adverse events in a full‑risk model. | | **Financial** | • Tight margin: 4–5% on top of national average cost.
• Exposure to catastrophic episodes (e.g., a single patient with $200k+ hospital stay).
• Need for stop‑loss or carve‑out mechanisms. | --- ## 3. Deal‑structure elements that make the contract defensible | Element | What it should include | Why it matters | |---------|------------------------|----------------| | **Base capitation rate** | $1,180 PMPM *plus* a risk‑adjusted component (e.g., HCC multiplier). | Aligns payment with patient acuity. | | **Risk adjustment** | • Use the payer’s HCC or CMS‑RAC model.
• Minimum guaranteed payment for high‑risk patients. | Prevents “cream‑skimming” and ensures sicker patients are compensated. | | **Quality bonuses & penalties** | • Tiered bonus structure (e.g., 1–3% of base revenue).
• Penalties capped at a percentage of total revenue.
• Clear definition of metrics, thresholds, and audit rights. | Incentivizes high performance while protecting against punitive over‑penalties. | | **Stop‑loss / carve‑out** | • Catastrophic stop‑loss (e.g., 5–10% of annual revenue).
• Carve‑out for patients with >$X per member cost.
• Option to transfer high‑cost episodes to a hospital partner. | Limits exposure to outlier claims that could wipe out margins. | | **Shared‑savings** | • If the group keeps costs below a target, it earns a share of savings (e.g., 50% of savings above target).
• Target set at risk‑adjusted cost baseline. | Encourages efficient care delivery and aligns incentives. | | **Performance escalation clause** | • Annual review of cap rate based on actual utilization & quality performance.
• Cap rate can be adjusted up/down by a defined percentage (e.g., ±5%). | Keeps the contract responsive to real‑world data. | | **Data sharing & audit rights** | • Payer provides monthly utilization, cost, and quality reports.
• Group has right to audit payer’s claims processing.
• Joint data governance committee. | Ensures transparency and early detection of discrepancies. | | **Compliance & indemnification** | • Payer indemnifies the group for Medicare compliance violations.
• Group indemnifies payer for claims arising from its clinical care.
• Both parties maintain adequate malpractice & liability insurance. | Protects both sides from legal exposure. | | **Governance structure** | • Joint steering committee (clinical, finance, compliance).
• Quarterly review meetings.
• Dispute‑resolution mechanism (mediation → arbitration). | Facilitates timely resolution of operational issues. | --- ## 4. Operational “must‑haves” for a full‑risk contract | Area | Action | |------|--------| | **Population health platform** | Deploy an integrated EHR + analytics system that tracks HEDIS metrics, risk scores, and care gaps in real time. | | **Care coordination team** | Hire or upskill 1–2 care managers per 5k members; include social workers for SDOH interventions. | | **Hospital & specialty network** | Negotiate preferred‑provider contracts with local hospitals and specialists; ensure timely referral pathways. | | **Clinical protocols** | Standardize chronic disease management (e.g., diabetes, COPD) to reduce ED visits and readmissions. | | **Quality improvement cycle** | Monthly dashboards for HEDIS metrics; quarterly quality review meetings; rapid‑cycle PDSA loops. | | **Risk‑adjusted reporting** | Build a data pipeline that feeds patient risk scores into the payer’s payment model each quarter. | --- ## 5. Financial viability: A quick “what‑if” scenario Assumptions (per member per month): | Item | Value | Comment | |------|-------|---------| | Base cap rate | $1,180 | As offered | | Risk‑adjusted add‑on | +$50 | For high‑risk patients (average 20% of panel) | | Quality bonus | +$30 | Average across HEDIS metrics | | Stop‑loss threshold | 5% of revenue | Caps catastrophic losses | **Estimated cost per member per month** (target): | Category | Cost | % of cap rate | |----------|------|---------------| | Primary care visits | $300 | 25% | | Specialty referrals | $200 | 17% | | Hospitalizations / ED | $400 | 34% | | Pharmacy & durable goods | $150 | 13% | | Care coordination & admin | $100 | 9% | Total estimated cost: **$1,050 /PMPM**. Margin before bonuses: **$130 /PMPM** (≈11%). If the group can keep actual costs ≤$1,050 /PMPM and earn the quality bonus, it will be profitable even after stop‑loss. If utilization spikes (e.g., a 10% increase in hospitalizations), the stop‑loss would absorb the excess. --- ## 6. Bottom line recommendation | Question | Answer | |----------|--------| | **Take the contract as written?** | *No.* The base rate is too high relative to the group’s expected cost unless you can shift risk or earn significant bonuses. | | **What must change for it to be defensible?** | • Add a robust risk‑adjustment component.
• Include stop‑loss and carve‑out provisions.
• Tie quality bonuses to clear, attainable metrics with capped penalties.
• Build in shared‑savings and escalation clauses.
• Ensure legal indemnification and compliance safeguards. | | **What operational investments are required?** | • Population health analytics platform.
• Care coordination workforce.
• Hospital/specialty network agreements.
• Quality improvement infrastructure. | | **Financial viability threshold?** | Keep total cost ≤$1,050 /PMPM (≈$30 M/month) and earn at least a 2–3% quality bonus to maintain an 8–10% margin after stop‑loss. | If the group can negotiate those changes—especially a risk‑adjusted payment model and a meaningful stop‑loss cap—it could be a lucrative opportunity that also positions the practice as a leader in value‑based care. If not, it’s safer to decline or renegotiate for a more traditional fee‑for‑service arrangement until the necessary infrastructure is in place.
